putnam-1988-a1.title: Use the symmetry and integrate over y
putnam-1988-a1.body:
The conditions only involve $|x|$ and $|y|$, so $R$ is symmetric about both axes. In the first quadrant ($x,y\ge 0$) the conditions read
$$0 \le y \le 1, \qquad 0 \le x \le 1 + y .$$
So for each height $y\in[0,1]$ the horizontal cross-section has length $1+y$, and the first-quadrant part has area
$$\int_0^1 (1+y)\,dy = 1 + \tfrac12 = \tfrac32 .$$
(It is the trapezoid with vertices $(0,0),(1,0),(2,1),(0,1)$.)

**Sketch.** Reflecting in both axes, $R$ is the (non-convex) hexagon with vertices
$$(1,0),\ (2,1),\ (-2,1),\ (-1,0),\ (-2,-1),\ (2,-1),$$
i.e. the rectangle $[-2,2]\times[-1,1]$ with a triangular notch cut into the middle of its left and right sides, the notches pointing in to $(\pm1,0)$.

**Area:** $4\cdot\frac32 = 6$.

**Answer: 6**

putnam-1988-a1.title: Rectangle minus two notches
putnam-1988-a1.body:
Since $|y|\le 1$, the condition $|x| \le 1+|y|$ gives $|x|\le 2$, so $R$ lies in the rectangle $[-2,2]\times[-1,1]$ of area $8$.

A point of the rectangle with $x>0$ is missing from $R$ exactly when $x > 1 + |y|$. That set is the triangle with vertices $(1,0)$, $(2,1)$, $(2,-1)$ (minus part of its boundary), of area $\frac12\cdot 2\cdot 1 = 1$. By symmetry the same triangle is missing on the left.

So the area of $R$ is $8 - 1 - 1 = 6$.

**Answer: 6**

putnam-1988-a2.title: Solve the separable differential equation
putnam-1988-a2.body:
We look for $g$ with $f'g + fg' = f'g'$, where $f = e^{x^2}$ and $f' = 2xe^{x^2}$. Dividing by $e^{x^2}>0$, the equation becomes
$$2x\,g + g' = 2x\,g' \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad (2x-1)\,g' = 2x\,g .$$
On the interval $(\tfrac12,\infty)$ (where $2x-1>0$) a positive solution must satisfy
$$\frac{g'}{g} = \frac{2x}{2x-1} = 1 + \frac{1}{2x-1}, \qquad\text{so}\qquad \ln g = x + \tfrac12\ln(2x-1) + C .$$
This suggests $g(x) = e^{x}\sqrt{2x-1}$ on $(a,b) = (\tfrac12, \infty)$ (any bounded subinterval also works).

**Check.** $g'(x) = e^x\sqrt{2x-1} + \dfrac{e^x}{\sqrt{2x-1}} = \dfrac{e^x\,(2x-1+1)}{\sqrt{2x-1}} = \dfrac{2x\,e^x}{\sqrt{2x-1}}$. Then
$$f'g' = 2xe^{x^2}\cdot\frac{2xe^x}{\sqrt{2x-1}} = \frac{4x^2e^{x^2+x}}{\sqrt{2x-1}},$$
$$(fg)' = f'g + fg' = e^{x^2+x}\Big(2x\sqrt{2x-1} + \frac{2x}{\sqrt{2x-1}}\Big) = e^{x^2+x}\,\frac{2x(2x-1) + 2x}{\sqrt{2x-1}} = \frac{4x^2e^{x^2+x}}{\sqrt{2x-1}} .$$
They agree on $(\tfrac12,\infty)$, and $g$ is nonzero there.

**Answer: Yes** — e.g. $g(x) = e^x\sqrt{2x-1}$ on $(\tfrac12,\infty)$.

putnam-1988-a3.title: Compare the terms with a p-series
putnam-1988-a3.body:
Write $t = 1/n\in(0,1]$ and $u_n = \frac{t}{\sin t} - 1 = \frac{t - \sin t}{\sin t}$. Since $0<\sin t<t$, we have $u_n>0$, so $u_n^x$ is defined for every real $x$.

**Two-sided estimate.** From the alternating Taylor series (whose terms decrease in size for $0<t\le 1$),
$$t - \frac{t^3}{6} \le \sin t \le t - \frac{t^3}{6} + \frac{t^5}{120}, \qquad\text{so}\qquad \frac{t^3}{6} - \frac{t^5}{120} \le t - \sin t \le \frac{t^3}{6}.$$
Also $\frac{5t}{6}\le t-\frac{t^3}{6} \le \sin t \le t$. Hence
$$u_n \ge \frac{t^3/6 - t^5/120}{t} = \frac{t^2}{6}\Big(1-\frac{t^2}{20}\Big) \ge \frac{19}{120}\,t^2, \qquad u_n \le \frac{t^3/6}{5t/6} = \frac{t^2}{5}.$$
So $c_1/n^2 \le u_n \le c_2/n^2$ with $c_1 = \frac{19}{120}$, $c_2 = \frac15$, and both $< 1$.

**Case $x>0$.** Raising to the power $x$ preserves inequalities: $c_1^x n^{-2x} \le u_n^x \le c_2^x n^{-2x}$. By comparison with $\sum n^{-2x}$, the series converges iff $2x>1$, i.e. $x>\frac12$.

**Case $x\le 0$.** Since $0<u_n<1$, we get $u_n^x \ge 1$ for all $n$, so the terms do not tend to $0$ and the series diverges.

**Answer:** the series converges exactly for $x\in(\tfrac12,\infty)$. ∎

putnam-1988-a4.title: Equilateral triangles for (a), a square tiling for (b)
putnam-1988-a4.body:
Measure distances in inches.

**(a) Yes.** Suppose, for contradiction, that the plane is 3-colored with no two points of the same color at distance $1$.

*Step 1.* Any equilateral triangle of side $1$ then has its three vertices in three different colors.

*Step 2.* Let $P,Q$ be any two points with $|PQ| = \sqrt3$. A rhombus made of two unit equilateral triangles glued along a side has long diagonal $2\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2} = \sqrt3$, so there are points $X, Y$ (the ends of the short diagonal, on the perpendicular bisector of $PQ$ at distance $\frac12$ from its midpoint) with $|XY| = 1$ and $|XP|=|YP|=|XQ|=|YQ|=1$. Triangles $PXY$ and $QXY$ are equilateral with side $1$, so by Step 1 both $P$ and $Q$ get the unique color different from the colors of $X$ and $Y$. Thus **any two points at distance $\sqrt3$ have the same color.**

*Step 3.* Fix a point $O$ and the circle of radius $\sqrt3$ around it. By Step 2 every point on that circle has the color of $O$. The circle has diameter $2\sqrt3 > 1$, so it contains two points at distance exactly $1$ — same color, contradiction.

**(b) No.** Let $s = \frac23$ and split the plane into half-open squares
$$Q_{i,j} = [is,(i+1)s)\times[js,(j+1)s), \qquad i,j\in\mathbb Z,$$
and give $Q_{i,j}$ the color $(i \bmod 3,\ j \bmod 3)$ — nine colors.

- Two points in the same square are at distance less than the diagonal $s\sqrt2 = \frac{2\sqrt2}{3} < 1$.
- Two points in different squares of the same color: then $i\equiv i'$, $j\equiv j' \pmod 3$ and $(i,j)\neq(i',j')$, so say $i' \ge i+3$ (or the same for $j$). Their $x$-coordinates satisfy $x' - x > i's - (i+1)s \ge 2s = \frac43 > 1$, so their distance exceeds $1$.

Hence no two points of the same color are exactly $1$ apart.

**Answer:** (a) yes; (b) no. ∎

putnam-1988-a5.title: Iterate and solve the linear recurrence
putnam-1988-a5.body:
**Existence.** $f(x) = 2x$ maps $\mathbb R^+$ to $\mathbb R^+$ and $f(f(x)) = 4x = 6x - 2x$.

**Uniqueness.** Let $f$ be any such function and fix $x>0$. Define $a_0 = x$ and $a_{n+1} = f(a_n)$; all $a_n>0$. Applying the functional equation at the point $a_n$ gives
$$a_{n+2} = 6a_n - a_{n+1}\qquad (n\ge 0).$$
The characteristic equation $r^2 + r - 6 = 0$ has roots $r = 2$ and $r=-3$, so there are constants $\alpha,\beta$ with
$$a_n = \alpha\, 2^n + \beta\,(-3)^n \quad\text{for all } n\ge 0$$
(the constants are determined by $a_0, a_1$, and both sides satisfy the same recurrence).

If $\beta \ne 0$, then $a_n/3^n = \alpha(2/3)^n + \beta(-1)^n$, and since $(2/3)^n\to 0$, for large $n$ this has the sign of $\beta(-1)^n$, which alternates. So some $a_n$ would be negative — impossible. Hence $\beta = 0$, $a_n = \alpha 2^n$, and $a_0 = x$ gives $\alpha = x$. In particular
$$f(x) = a_1 = 2x .$$
As $x>0$ was arbitrary, $f(x)=2x$ is the only solution. ∎

putnam-1988-a6.title: Expand the extra eigenvector in the basis
putnam-1988-a6.body:
Let the eigenvectors be $v_1,\dots,v_{n+1}$ with $Av_i = \lambda_i v_i$ (eigenvectors are nonzero).

Since $v_1,\dots,v_n$ are linearly independent in an $n$-dimensional space, they form a basis, so
$$v_{n+1} = c_1v_1 + \cdots + c_nv_n .$$
**Every $c_j\neq 0$:** if $c_j = 0$, this equation would be a linear dependence among the $n$ vectors $v_{n+1}$ and $v_i$ ($i\ne j$, $i \le n$), contrary to the hypothesis.

Apply $A$:
$$\lambda_{n+1}\sum_{i=1}^n c_iv_i = A v_{n+1} = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i\lambda_i v_i .$$
Comparing coefficients in the basis, $c_i(\lambda_i - \lambda_{n+1}) = 0$, hence $\lambda_i = \lambda_{n+1} =: \lambda$ for every $i$.

So $A v_i = \lambda v_i$ for all vectors of a basis, which means $A = \lambda I$.

**Answer: Yes**, $A$ must be a scalar multiple of the identity. ∎

putnam-1988-b1.title: Choose z = 1
putnam-1988-b1.body:
With $z = 1$ the expression becomes
$$xy + x + y + 1 = (x+1)(y+1).$$
So given a composite $ab$ with $a,b\ge 2$, take $x = a-1\ge 1$, $y = b-1 \ge 1$, $z = 1$. These are positive integers and
$$xy + xz + yz + 1 = (a-1)(b-1) + (a-1) + (b-1) + 1 = ab .$$
∎

putnam-1988-b2.title: Bound |x| from below
putnam-1988-b2.body:
The statement is **true**.

If $0\le y\le 1$, then $y(y-1)\le 0\le x^2$ and we are done. So assume $y>1$, and put $s = \sqrt{y^2+y}$; then $s>\sqrt2>1$.

The hypothesis says $|x+1| \ge s$. By the triangle inequality $|x| \ge |x+1| - 1 \ge s-1 > 0$, so
$$x^2 \ge (s-1)^2 = y^2 + y - 2s + 1 .$$
Now $4s^2 = 4y^2+4y < (2y+1)^2$, so $2s < 2y+1$. Therefore
$$x^2 > y^2 + y - (2y+1) + 1 = y^2 - y = y(y-1).$$
∎ **Answer: True.**

putnam-1988-b2.title: Square-root inequality
putnam-1988-b2.body:
Again the case $0\le y\le1$ is trivial, so let $y>1$. The claim is $|x| \ge \sqrt{y^2-y}$, and the hypothesis gives $|x| \ge |x+1|-1 \ge \sqrt{y^2+y} - 1$. So it suffices to show
$$\sqrt{y^2+y} - 1 \ge \sqrt{y^2-y}, \qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \sqrt{y^2+y} - \sqrt{y^2-y} \ge 1 .$$
Rationalising,
$$\sqrt{y^2+y} - \sqrt{y^2-y} = \frac{2y}{\sqrt{y^2+y} + \sqrt{y^2-y}} > \frac{2y}{(y+\frac12) + (y-\frac12)} = 1,$$
using $\sqrt{y^2\pm y} < y \pm \frac12$ (square both sides: $y^2\pm y < y^2 \pm y + \frac14$). ∎ **Answer: True.**

putnam-1988-b3.title: Distance to the nearest multiple of 1+√3, plus Pell's equation
putnam-1988-b3.body:
Put $\theta = 1+\sqrt3$. With $c = n-d$ we get $|c - d\sqrt3| = |n - d\theta|$, so
$$r_n = \min_{0\le d\le n} |n - d\theta| .$$
The integer $d$ nearest to $n/\theta$ lies in $[0,n]$ (because $0<n/\theta<n$), so $r_n = \theta\cdot\|n/\theta\|$, where $\|t\|$ denotes the distance from $t$ to the nearest integer.

**Upper bound, never attained.** $\|t\|\le\frac12$, with equality only if $t\in\frac12+\mathbb Z$. But $n/\theta = \frac{n(\sqrt3-1)}2$ is irrational, so $r_n < \frac{\theta}{2}$ for every $n$.

**The bound is approached.** Take the solutions of $m^2 - 3n^2 = 1$ given by $m + n\sqrt3 = (2+\sqrt3)^k$, $k = 1,2,\dots$; they have $n\to\infty$. Here $m$ and $n$ have opposite parity: both even is impossible since $m^2-3n^2$ is odd, and both odd gives $m^2 - 3n^2 \equiv 1 - 3 \equiv 6 \pmod 8$. Let $\varepsilon = m - n\sqrt3 = \frac{1}{m+n\sqrt3}$, so $0<\varepsilon\to0$. Then
$$\frac n\theta = \frac{n\sqrt3 - n}{2} = \frac{m-n}{2} - \frac{\varepsilon}{2},$$
and $\frac{m-n}2$ is a half-odd-integer, so $\|n/\theta\| = \frac12-\frac\varepsilon2$ and $r_n = \frac\theta2 - \frac{\theta\varepsilon}{2} \to \frac\theta2$.

Hence $\sup_n r_n = \frac{\theta}2$, and the smallest $g$ with $r_n\le g$ for all $n$ is
$$g = \frac{1+\sqrt3}{2}.$$
**Answer:** $g = \dfrac{1+\sqrt3}{2}$. ∎

putnam-1988-b4.title: Split into large and small terms
putnam-1988-b4.body:
Fix $n$ and write $a_n^{n/(n+1)} = a_n\cdot a_n^{-1/(n+1)}$.

- If $a_n \ge 2^{-(n+1)}$, then $a_n^{-1/(n+1)} \le \big(2^{-(n+1)}\big)^{-1/(n+1)} = 2$, so $a_n^{n/(n+1)} \le 2a_n$.
- If $a_n < 2^{-(n+1)}$, then $a_n^{n/(n+1)} < 2^{-n}$ (the map $t\mapsto t^{n/(n+1)}$ is increasing).

In either case $0 < a_n^{n/(n+1)} \le 2a_n + 2^{-n}$. Since $\sum a_n$ and $\sum 2^{-n}$ converge, the comparison test shows $\sum a_n^{n/(n+1)}$ converges. ∎

putnam-1988-b4.title: Weighted AM–GM (Young's inequality)
putnam-1988-b4.body:
For $u,v\ge0$ and weights $\frac{n}{n+1}+\frac1{n+1} = 1$, weighted AM–GM gives $u^{n/(n+1)}v^{1/(n+1)} \le \frac{n}{n+1}u + \frac1{n+1}v \le u+v$.

Take $u = 2a_n$ and $v = 2^{-n}$. The powers of $2$ cancel, $2^{n/(n+1)}\cdot 2^{-n/(n+1)} = 1$, so
$$a_n^{n/(n+1)} = (2a_n)^{n/(n+1)}(2^{-n})^{1/(n+1)} \le 2a_n + 2^{-n}.$$ Summing, $\sum a_n^{n/(n+1)} \le 2\sum a_n + 1 < \infty$. ∎

putnam-1988-b5.title: Odd skew-symmetric determinant, then work mod 2
putnam-1988-b5.body:
**Rank $\le 2n$.** For a skew-symmetric matrix of odd size $N=2n+1$,
$$\det M_n = \det M_n^{T} = \det(-M_n) = (-1)^{2n+1}\det M_n = -\det M_n,$$
so $\det M_n = 0$ and the rank is at most $2n$.

**Rank $\ge 2n$.** Let $N'$ be the upper-left $2n\times 2n$ submatrix. Its diagonal entries are $0$ and every off-diagonal entry is $\pm1\equiv 1 \pmod 2$. So modulo $2$, $N' \equiv J - I$, where $J$ is the all-ones $2n\times 2n$ matrix. The eigenvalues of $J - I$ are $2n-1$ (eigenvector $(1,\dots,1)$) and $-1$ with multiplicity $2n-1$, so
$$\det(J-I) = (2n-1)(-1)^{2n-1} = -(2n-1),$$
which is odd. The determinant is a polynomial with integer coefficients in the entries, so $\det N' \equiv \det(J - I) \equiv 1 \pmod 2$. Hence $\det N'$ is odd, in particular nonzero.

**Answer:** $\operatorname{rank} M_n = 2n$. ∎

putnam-1988-b6.title: Use the criterion 8N+1 = square
putnam-1988-b6.body:
**Lemma.** A nonnegative integer $N$ is triangular if and only if $8N+1$ is a perfect square.

*Proof.* If $N = \frac{m(m+1)}2$, then $8N+1 = 4m^2+4m+1 = (2m+1)^2$. Conversely, if $8N+1 = s^2$ with $s\ge 0$, then $s$ is odd, $s = 2m+1$ with $m\ge0$, and $N = \frac{s^2-1}{8} = \frac{m(m+1)}{2}$. $\square$

**Construction.** For $k = 1,2,3,\dots$ let
$$a = (2k+1)^2, \qquad b = \frac{k(k+1)}{2} = \frac{a-1}{8}.$$
These pairs are pairwise distinct, so there are infinitely many. For any positive integer $t$, $at+b\ge 0$ and
$$8(at+b) + 1 = 8at + a = (2k+1)^2\,(8t+1).$$
- If $t$ is triangular, $8t+1 = s^2$, so $8(at+b)+1 = \big((2k+1)s\big)^2$ is a square and $at+b$ is triangular.
- If $at+b$ is triangular, $(2k+1)^2(8t+1) = u^2$ for an integer $u$. Then $8t+1 = \big(\frac{u}{2k+1}\big)^2$ is the square of a rational number; an integer that is the square of a rational is the square of an integer (if $p/q$ is in lowest terms and $q>1$, then $p^2/q^2$ is not an integer). So $8t+1$ is a perfect square and $t$ is triangular.

Hence each pair $(a,b)$ has the required property. (For example $k=1$ gives $9t+1$: $9\cdot\frac{n(n+1)}{2} + 1 = \frac{(3n+1)(3n+2)}{2}$.) ∎
